title: (Scenario) Pods are `Running` but not receiving traffic via the Ingress/Service — walk through the layers (readiness probe, Service selector/endpoints, Ingress rules, NetworkPolicy, LB health checks).
shortTitle: (Scenario) Pods Are Running but Receive No Traffic Through Ingress/Service

s1_definition.profdef: When Pods are Running but get no traffic, the containers are healthy yet something between the client and the Pod is broken. The diagnosis walks the request path layer by layer: the readiness probe must pass so the Pod is marked Ready, the Service selector must match the Pod labels so the EndpointSlice lists the Pod IP, the Ingress host and path rules must point at the right Service and port, any NetworkPolicy must allow the traffic, and the external load balancer health checks must consider the backend healthy.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India the teller is at the desk and ready to serve, but no customers arrive. The teller being present is "Running." The missing customers could be because the OPEN sign never flipped on (readiness), the branch directory lists the wrong desk number (Service selector and endpoints), the reception sends "transfers" visitors to the wrong floor (Ingress rules), a security door blocks the corridor (NetworkPolicy), or the building's front-gate guard marked this branch "closed" on his sheet (load balancer health check). You check each checkpoint from the street inward until you find the broken one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Running means the container is alive, not reachable; trace readiness, Service selector and endpoints, Ingress rules, NetworkPolicy, and load balancer health checks until you find the gap.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When Pods are Running but get no traffic, the containers are healthy yet something between the client and the Pod is broken. The diagnosis walks the request path layer by layer: the readiness probe must pass so the Pod is marked Ready, the Service selector must match the Pod labels so the EndpointSlice lists the Pod IP, the Ingress host and path rules must point at the right Service and port, any NetworkPolicy must allow the traffic, and the external load balancer health checks must consider the backend healthy.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India the teller is at the desk and ready to serve, but no customers arrive. The teller being present is "Running." The missing customers could be because the OPEN sign never flipped on (readiness), the branch directory lists the wrong desk number (Service selector and endpoints), the reception sends "transfers" visitors to the wrong floor (Ingress rules), a security door blocks the corridor (NetworkPolicy), or the building's front-gate guard marked this branch "closed" on his sheet (load balancer health check). You check each checkpoint from the street inward until you find the broken one.

**One line to remember:** Running means the container is alive, not reachable; trace readiness, Service selector and endpoints, Ingress rules, NetworkPolicy, and load balancer health checks until you find the gap.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with readiness, because a Running Pod whose readiness probe fails is deliberately kept out of the Service. I run `kubectl get pods` and look at the READY column; if it shows 0/1 even though STATUS is Running, the readiness probe is failing and the Pod is correctly excluded from traffic. The fix is to make the readiness endpoint pass.

Next check the Service selector and endpoints. The Service selects Pods by labels, and the EndpointSlice controller lists the IPs of matching ready Pods. If the Service selector is `app=transfer` but the Pods are labelled `app=transfer-service`, the selector matches nothing and the endpoint list is empty, so traffic has nowhere to go. I run `kubectl get endpointslices` or `kubectl describe service` and confirm the endpoint list is non-empty and contains the Pod IPs. An empty list is the single most common cause and usually traces back to a label mismatch or failing readiness.

Then verify the Service plumbing itself: the Service `port` versus `targetPort` must match the container's actual listening port. A Service forwarding port 80 to targetPort 8080 only works if the container listens on 8080. I test inside the cluster with a temporary Pod doing `curl http://transfer-service:80` to isolate whether the Service works before blaming the Ingress.

Next the Ingress. The Ingress host and path rules must name the correct Service and port, and the Ingress controller must actually be running and have an address. I run `kubectl describe ingress` to confirm the backend is the right Service and `kubectl get ingress` to confirm it has an external address. A wrong service name, a path that does not match, or a missing IngressClass are typical breaks.

Then NetworkPolicy. In a locked-down banking namespace a default-deny policy can block ingress to the Pods unless an explicit allow rule permits traffic from the Ingress controller's namespace or Pod labels. I check `kubectl get networkpolicy` and confirm there is an allow rule for the relevant source.

Finally the external load balancer health checks. For a LoadBalancer Service or a cloud Ingress, the cloud load balancer runs its own health checks against the node ports or target group. If those health checks hit a path that returns non-200, the load balancer marks the backend unhealthy and sends no traffic even though Kubernetes thinks everything is fine. I check the cloud target group health in the provider console. The senior discipline is to test from the inside out: curl the Pod IP directly, then the Service, then through the Ingress, then from outside, so each hop tells you whether the break is below or above it.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our Transfer Service Pods were Running after a deploy, but the mobile app got timeouts. The scenario reproduces the layered walk that found the break.

Problem 1 — a refactor renamed the Pod label from `app=transfer` to `app=transfer-svc`, but the Service selector still said `app=transfer`, so the endpoint list was empty and no traffic flowed even though Pods were Running and Ready. This is the classic selector mismatch.

Problem 2 — separately, a readiness probe pointed at the wrong path returned 404, so Pods showed 0/1 Ready and were excluded. Both faults produce the same symptom, which is why a layered walk is essential.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `TrafficPathChecker` that models each layer: readiness, Service selector versus Pod labels and the resulting endpoints, Ingress backend mapping, NetworkPolicy allow rules, and load balancer health. It walks the layers in order, reports the first broken one with the fix, and once every layer is healthy routes a transfer for Rajesh and Priya to prove traffic reaches the Pod.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Running, Ready Pod labelled `app=transfer-svc`, first fronted by a Service whose selector wrongly says `app=transfer`, then by a corrected Service.

Step 1 — Layer 1 readiness: the Pod is Ready, so it is not excluded for readiness reasons. The walk continues.

Step 2 — Layer 2 endpoints: the Service selector `app=transfer` is compared to the Pod labels `app=transfer-svc`. They do not match, so the endpoint list is empty. The checker reports the empty-endpoints break and the fix to align the selector, and stops. This reproduces the real outage: Pods Running and Ready, yet zero traffic.

Step 3 — We apply the fix by using a Service whose selector is `app=transfer-svc`. The walk runs again. Readiness passes, the selector now matches so the endpoint list contains the Pod IP, and the targetPort 8080 matches the container's listen port.

Step 4 — Layer 3 Ingress: the Ingress backend names `transfer-service`, which matches the actual Service, so routing is correct. Layer 4 NetworkPolicy allows ingress from the controller. Layer 5 load balancer health check passes.

Step 5 — Every layer is healthy, so traffic reaches the Pod IP. A transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya is routed to the Pod and succeeds, proving the end-to-end path is restored.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When Pods are Running but receive no traffic, the containers themselves are healthy and the fault lies somewhere between the client and the Pod, so I walk the request path layer by layer rather than guessing. My golden rule is to test from the inside out: curl the Pod directly, then the Service, then through the Ingress, then from outside, because each successful hop tells me the break is above it and each failed hop tells me the break is at or below it.

I start with readiness, because a Running Pod whose readiness probe is failing is deliberately excluded from the Service and shows zero-slash-one in the ready column. Next I check the Service selector against the Pod labels and look at the endpoint list, because an empty endpoint list is by far the most common cause and almost always traces back to a label mismatch or failing readiness. While there, I confirm the Service target port matches the container's real listening port. Then I inspect the Ingress to make sure its host and path rules point at the correct Service and port and that the Ingress controller actually has an address. After that I check for a default-deny NetworkPolicy that blocks ingress from the controller, which is common in locked-down banking namespaces. Finally I check the external load balancer's own health checks, because a cloud load balancer that gets a non-200 from its health path will mark the backend unhealthy and send no traffic even though Kubernetes believes everything is fine.

The reason this layered approach matters is that several completely different faults produce the exact same symptom of Running Pods with no traffic, so a methodical walk is faster and safer than trial and error. In my project at the National Bank of India a refactor renamed the Pod label but left the Service selector pointing at the old label, so the endpoint list went empty and the mobile app timed out even though every Pod was Running and Ready. Aligning the Service selector with the new Pod labels restored the endpoints instantly and traffic flowed again. That incident is exactly why I always inspect endpoints early and verify each layer in order instead of restarting Pods that were never actually broken.
